slides.title: Introduction
slides.content: Introduction • This course: learning to program, using the Python programming language • Goal: write your own programs to collect, process and analyze data, with a focus on ‘humanities’ research: text, tables, data from the web • No prior programming experience assumed • Along the way: a way of thinking (computational, algorithmic) that carries over to any other programming language • But main focus: getting things done 2/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Scripting languages?
slides.content: Scripting languages? • Programming languages vs. scripting languages • Programming language: code needs to be compiled before it can be run • Scripting language: code can be executed on the fly, without compilation • Difference is becoming less and less important as compilation on modern hardware can often be done very fast, on the fly • Scripting: light-weight, easy to use piece of code to automate a specific task • Hands on attitude to programming • Ease of development more important than fast programs • Focus on digital humanities: scripting for text processing and humanities data 3/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Scripting languages = Python
slides.content: Scripting languages = Python • In practice, main focus of the course will be: learning to program in Python • Easy and intuitive language • Code is easily understandable (similar to plain English) • Many useful libraries are available (particularly for data science) 4/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Computers for DH research?
slides.content: Computers for DH research? • Computers allow us • to automate (avoid boring work) • to amplify (analyze more data than human can handle) • to reproduce (share data and code along with publications) 14/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Programming for DH research?
slides.content: Programming for DH research? To process data automatically, we can: • Use existing tools or programs • limited to existing functionality • often difficult to repeat a sequence of actions • Create our own programs/scripts • Higher investment to get started • But endless opportunities 15/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Learning to program in 2026
slides.content: Learning to program in 2026 • Large language models can write Python. So why learn it? • Programming knowledge allows you to specify your needs more precisely • You have to judge whether the result is correct: generated code often looks right and is subtly wrong • You have to debug when it fails, on your data, on your machine • You cannot take responsibility when you have no idea what goes on under the hood! • Advice for the first weeks: type the code yourself, and use AI tools to explain, not to solve 16/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Python is a language
slides.content: Python is a language A language has: • words: primitive constructs, basic building blocks of the language • syntax: rules that stipulate how words combine • semantics: the meaning that is derived from the words and the way they are combined 17/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Learning a language
slides.content: Learning a language • Learning Python is like learning a language • You will (and need to!) make mistakes • Syntactic errors • common and easily caught • Semantic errors • Python will check for significant semantic anomalies • Subtle semantic differences can cause unexpected behaviour • Ambiguity • No error, but meaning is different from what programmer intended • Script crashes, script runs forever, script returns a different answer than expected, … 22/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Python script
slides.content: Python script • a script is a sequence of definitions and commands • definitions are evaluated • commands are executed by Python interpreter in a shell • commands (statements) instruct interpreter to do something • can be typed directly in a shell or stored in a file that is read into the shell and evaluated 23/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Objects
slides.content: Objects • A script manipulates data objects • Objects have a type that defines the kinds of things programs can do to them • a banana is of type fruit so it can be eaten, peeled, etc. • Kim is of type human so she can walk, speak, etc. • Objects are: • scalar (cannot be subdivided) • non-scalar (have internal structure that can be accessed) 24/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: How to run Python code?
slides.content: How to run Python code? • Two-step process: edit code, then run • Write entire script, and save in a file • Give file to Python interpreter to execute • (Solve errors and repeat) • Interactive shell • Launch interactive Python shell • Type commands directly into shell • Notebook • Most interactive way to run Python code • Notebook combines explanatory text, code, and results • Interface through web browser • User-friendly version provided by Google: Google Colab (https://colab.research.google.com) 25/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Installing Python
slides.content: Installing Python • Main Python release • Available at http://www.python.org • Can be somewhat cumbersome to use, particularly under Windows • Anaconda distribution (recommended) • Available at https://www.anaconda.com/download • User-friendly distribution • Suitable for data science and machine learning • Simplifies package management and code execution • Comes with Jupyter Notebook, which we use in the practical sessions • Note: installation process (and which installer to download) depends on your operating system 26/28 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
